opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Most of the conversation about AI's environmental impact has focused on training. People cite how much energy it took to train some huge model, and those numbers are striking. But training happens once, or a handful of times. Once a model is deployed, it can be queried millions or even billions of times a day, and that adds up very quickly. For widely used models, the cumulative cost of inference can match or exceed the cost of training within weeks or months.

There was also a real gap in the research. Training costs have at least been somewhat documented, partly because researchers sometimes report them in papers. Deployment was a black box. Companies weren't disclosing it, and there wasn't a systematic way of comparing tasks or model types. So we set out to measure it: we took a range of models, from small task-specific ones to large general-purpose generative ones, ran them on the same hardware across different tasks, and tracked energy use and carbon emissions per query.

One of the clearest findings was that generative tasks, especially image generation, are far more energy-intensive than classification-type tasks. Multipurpose generative models also use a lot more energy than smaller models fine-tuned for a specific task, even when both do the same thing. That matters because there's a trend toward using one giant model for everything, sometimes when a much smaller, more efficient model would work fine.

So focusing on deployment was about following where the energy is actually going as AI becomes part of everyday products, and giving people better information to make choices. Developers can choose which model to deploy, and users and policymakers can push for transparency. Right now we're flying a bit blind, and I'd like to change that.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts one-time training with ongoing deployment queries and says deployment was a black box, but it does not explain that the ongoing workload is why deployment energy is harder to measure.

r002.rationale: It gives no estimate of 50 million to 200 million queries for text-generation models.

r003.rationale: It says image generation is energy-intensive, but does not state that inference for production image-generation models has a much larger long-term climate cost than training.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, there had been a fair amount of work done on the training side already, including some of my own. We'd looked at BLOOM, we'd estimated the carbon footprint of training large language models, and there were a few other papers out there doing that. But training is a one-time cost. You train a model once, maybe a few times with different runs, and then that's it. Deployment, on the other hand, is ongoing. Once a model is out in the world and people are using it, every single query consumes energy, and that keeps happening for as long as the model is in use. So when you think about the total lifecycle of a model, inference can actually end up dwarfing training, especially for models that are deployed at scale to millions of users.

The other thing was that nobody had really looked at it systematically. There was a lot of anecdotal discussion, people saying a ChatGPT query uses this many times more energy than a Google search, but there wasn't much empirical measurement across different types of models and tasks. So we wanted to actually sit down and measure it. We took a bunch of models from the Hugging Face Hub, across different modalities, text classification, question answering, image generation, and so on, and we ran them on the same hardware and measured the energy consumption per query. And what we found was that the variation is enormous. Image generation is orders of magnitude more energy-intensive than text classification, and general-purpose models are much more expensive than task-specific ones for the same task. That felt like important information for people who are making decisions about what to deploy.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts one-time training with ongoing per-query deployment and notes limited systematic measurement, but it does not clearly say deployment energy is harder to measure because of that ongoing workload.

r002.rationale: The response gives no estimate of 50 million to 200 million queries or equivalent figure.

r003.rationale: It says inference can dwarf training at scale and that image generation is energy-intensive per query, but does not state that image-generation inference has a much larger long-term climate cost than training.

astra-6.text:
We focused on deployment because that’s the part that happens over and over again. Training a model can take a lot of energy, but once it’s trained, it might be used millions of times a day. So, depending on how much it’s used, the energy required to run it can end up exceeding the energy used to train it.

There had also been a lot more attention paid to training, whereas we had much less visibility into the cost of using these systems. We wanted to understand what happens when you actually ask a model a question or generate an image, and how that energy use varies across tasks and models.

r001.rationale: The response says deployment happens repeatedly and has less visibility, but does not explain that measuring its energy is harder because production workloads are ongoing rather than bounded.

r002.rationale: It gives no query-count estimate for text-generation models.

r003.rationale: It says deployment energy can exceed training energy depending on usage, but does not state that image-generation inference has a much larger long-term climate cost than training.

sol-6.1.text:
We focused on deployment because that’s where a model gets used over and over again. Training can take a lot of energy, but it’s a finite process. Once you deploy a model, potentially millions of people are interacting with it, and each interaction has an energy cost. Over time, that can really add up.

There’s also been much more attention paid to the energy used in training than to inference. We wanted to understand what it costs to actually use these systems, and how that varies across different tasks and models.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts finite training with ongoing deployment use, but does not say that deployment energy is harder to measure.

r002.rationale: It gives no estimate of how many queries would consume energy equivalent to a training run.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss image-generation models or compare the long-term climate cost of inference with training.
